members.name: Bao Thien Ngo
members.title: cPALSs
members.vision: I want LNY to stay a place people show up as themselves — with creativity and passion, not more corporate hierarchy in nonprofit clothing. I gather visionaries who practice innovation. We merge calendars and introduce automation to give time back and create force multipliers across multiple visions. And I value honesty — even sharing our vulnerabilities — so peers get a real chance to step in and help.

members.name: Thuy Pham
members.title: VACOS
members.vision: What I love most is when a whole family shows up and everyone actually has something to do. Dad’s into tech, mom loves working with kids, their son is into animation — and each of them finds a place at the festival. A festival where there is something for everyone to do and enjoy. That’s the Tết I want us to put on.

members.name: Lily Tran
members.title: Lucky Wav
members.vision: If you grew up celebrating Lunar New Year, you know what it means to keep culture and tradition alive — and that each generation has its own way of expressing that. When I was asked to lead music for Elk Grove LNY, I got space to create something different. That’s how Lucky Wav was born: Lucky for blessings ahead, Wav for music, movement, and a new wave of culture. This segment is about honoring where we come from and celebrating where we’re headed — for our community in Sacramento and Elk Grove.

members.name: Ellie King
members.title: Tụ Vía Procession
members.vision: Saturday afternoon, we walk the Pavilion circle together. Tụ Vía — gathering vía as a community before Soul Torrent’s dusk. Lions, dance crews, banners, families in the ring. This year the procession is on foot: no cars, no floats. A walking circle we can staff well and enjoy. Street parades can wait until they’re properly funded.

visionFull.heading: Tụ Vía — walking circle, not a motor parade
paragraphs: I’m taking Soul Torrent’s afternoon chapter: Tụ Vía, the walking Obon-style circle at the Pavilion roundabout.
Guests gather vía together — lions, clubs, banners, families in the ring — then dusk is Spirit Break on the main stage. One Saturday product; two chapters.

Cars and floats in a parade are logistically heavy. For 2027 we scale that back. The park product is a walking procession we can actually run. A funded street parade is a later year, when we can staff and pay for it properly.

visionFull.heading: Honoring the History and Future of Chicano & Vietnamese Car Culture
paragraphs: The story of Chicano and Vietnamese collaboration is a beautiful reflection of California’s diverse communities coming together through shared experiences, creativity, and resilience.

Chicano culture has deep roots in California, shaped by generations of Mexican American families who built communities, fought for representation, and created powerful expressions of identity through art, music, fashion, and car culture. Lowriding became more than a style of automobiles — it became a form of storytelling, family tradition, craftsmanship, and cultural pride.

Following the Vietnam War, many Vietnamese refugees and immigrants made California their home, building new lives while preserving their traditions, language, food, and cultural identity. As Vietnamese communities grew throughout California, especially in areas with established Chicano communities, connections naturally developed through neighborhoods, schools, businesses, and shared community spaces.

Over time, both communities discovered common ground through entrepreneurship, family values, and automotive culture. Vietnamese car enthusiasts brought their own creativity through custom imports, performance builds, and unique expressions of automotive artistry, while Chicano communities continued the legacy of lowriders as symbols of heritage, pride, and connection. These different styles came together through mutual appreciation and respect.

Today, Chicano and Vietnamese car culture collaborations represent more than vehicles — they represent the power of communities recognizing their shared values. Car shows, cultural festivals, and community events have become places where generations can connect, stories can be exchanged, and traditions can be honored.

As the LNY Tết Festival Car Show Director and LNY Carshow Queen 2026, I am honored to help create a space where these cultures can celebrate side by side. This is how I envisioned our theme, East Meets West.

This vision was supported by Debbie “Tigerina” Martin and The Lady Lowriders United, whose dedication helped bring authenticity, passion, and community spirit to the celebration and the partnership of numerous car clubs.

My vision is to continue growing this car show as a bridge between cultures — a place where Chicano and Vietnamese communities can celebrate their history, inspire future generations, and show that our differences are not barriers, but opportunities to learn, connect, and build something stronger together.
Because at the heart of it all, it has never just been about cars. It has always been about people, stories, family, and community.

visionFull.heading: Resource Hub at LNY Tết Festival 2027
paragraphs: I’m Ellie King, The NonProfit Girl™.
I’ve spent most of my life serving my community, and one thing I know for sure is that real impact happens when real people come together with a shared heart and purpose.

My hope is to take our Resource Hub to LNY Tết — where culture, community, and resources come together; a place where celebration meets connection and where families can discover opportunities, support, and pathways to thrive.

My vision is to collaborate with churches, organizations, agencies, and service providers — where people can connect to learn about services, discover ways to give back, build partnerships, and find encouragement to turn their own ideas for helping others into action.

I don’t show up because I have all the answers. I show up because I care about people. The titles may say nonprofit CEO, consultant, or community advocate, but at my core, I’m simply a woman of faith, a wife, a mom, and a friend who believes that when we come together, we have the power to change lives.
Because community is built one connection, one conversation, and one act of kindness at a time.

directorIntro.title: What is a director?
paragraphs: A director (or DRI) is the accountable owner of one festival lane or Fund The Festival gift. You recommend and decide budget for your lane, including whether to contract out work. You recruit help, hire or place pros (paid or pro bono), and report status to the Steering Committee. You are not assumed to build sets, hang decor, or personally perform the craft.

Already covered: Steering Committee — Bao Thien Ngo (cPALSs) and Thuy Pham (VACOS). They hold coalition partnership-level decision authority. Tụ Vía Procession — Ellie King (walking circle; not a motor parade).

Open seats: 15 Program DRIs (Program gifts + Program & Entertainment umbrella), 6 Outreach Directors, an optional Site & Ops Chair, and Site & Ops Supercommittee members who claim workstreams as tasks demand. Soft gifts are sponsor unlocks. Returning 2026 volunteers are welcome — nothing is assumed until confirmed on the staff directory.
notes: Prefer one accountable DRI per Program gift. Multiple visionaries may share a lane as co-equals until a director coordinates them — see FAQ on Team.
Site & Ops is a supercommittee (optional Chair + Members), not separate Director titles per workstream.
Directors own budget and contracting decisions — craft labor is often hired.
Soft gifts (Relay Cup, Elders, Spread the Word, Cây Nêu) are sponsor unlocks — sponsor-gated or elective.
If a critical lane stays unfilled past the steering trigger date, a contractor fallback may be approved.

faq.q: What's the difference between a director and a visionary?
faq.a: A director / DRI is the accountable owner of a lane or Program gift — including budget and contracting decisions. A visionary owns a celebration vision and builds a crew around it — often along the journey to the weekend, not only day-of. Multiple visionaries can share a lane as co-equals until a director coordinates them.

faq.q: Do directors have to do the physical work?
faq.a: No. Directors decide budget and whether to hire contractors. Building sets, hang crew, stage production, and similar craft are often contracted. You own the outcome, not every task.

Generally not — these are volunteer leadership roles. We are open to contractors when a role or gift is funded. Full transparency: if you want paid marketing or similar work, we will likely ask you to pair that with a fundraising strategy and execute it to fund the role (and any campaign spend).
Helpful, not required. LNY 2026 runbooks and co-chairs back you up.

faq.q: What if my gift isn't funded yet?
faq.a: We operate as a network of owners. We put the word out when an experience is unfunded, but it is up to everyone to recruit help and spread the ask. We will create incentives so pitching in is worthwhile — gift registry blocks, sponsorship commission paths, and peer grapevine recruiting — not a single person carrying every fundraising ask.

about.headline: About Elk Grove Lunar New Year Tết

sections.title: Tết
paragraphs: Lunar New Year, known as Tết in Vietnamese culture, is one of the most significant and cherished celebrations in Asian communities worldwide. This ancient festival marks the beginning of the lunar calendar year and symbolizes renewal, family reunion, and hope for prosperity. For Vietnamese families, Tết represents a time to honor ancestors, strengthen family bonds, and welcome good fortune for the year ahead. Traditional celebrations include preparing special foods, decorating homes with flowers and symbols of luck, exchanging red envelopes (lì xì) for good fortune, and gathering with loved ones to reflect on the past year while embracing new beginnings.

For Vietnamese and Asian communities that fled after the Fall of Saigon following decades of war, arriving in America meant starting over in an unfamiliar land. As refugees worked to rebuild their livelihoods and establish new roots, Lunar New Year celebrations served a crucial function — providing a place of familiarity and community connection in their adopted homeland. This ancient tradition became more than just a cultural observance; it became an essential anchor that helped displaced families reorient themselves, maintain their identity, and forge bonds with fellow community members navigating similar challenges of resettlement.

sections.title: Sacramento & Elk Grove
paragraphs: Today, Elk Grove Lunar New Year Tết builds on decades of cultural celebrations in the Sacramento region — from Stockton Boulevard and Florin to Elk Grove Park. The festival is a free, family-centered gathering that welcomes the whole community: carnival, lion dance, multicultural programming, and live music.

The festival is co-hosted by Community Partners Advocate of Little Saigon Sacramento (cPALSs), Vietnamese American Community of Sacramento (VACOS), and Norcal Vietnamese Chamber of Commerce (NVCC), with generous support from sponsors, donors, and volunteers.
We hope you consider supporting our culturally-oriented and community-driven festival as part of this historical moment for our community.

sections.title: Soul Torrent
paragraphs: For 2027 we’re introducing Soul Torrent — a new theatrical festival concept for Saturday at Elk Grove Park. Too many festivals feel fragmented: random stage acts, random booths, random programming that never quite add up to a day you can tell someone about. Soul Torrent is our answer — one story guests can feel from daylight to dusk: dark spirits gather at the gates, protectors and families push back, and by dusk the crowd helps finish the fight.

Soul Torrent has two chapters under one name. In the afternoon, Tụ Vía invites guests into a walking circle — gathering vía (vital spirit) the way a community gathers strength together. At dusk, Spirit Break is the monsoon release: lions, heroes, music, and glow on the main stage as the malaise breaks and the park exhales before hard close.

Think of it as interactive theater woven through a free family fair — kids theater and village in daylight, teens and jackets for the dusk climax — not a nightclub and not a lecture on myth. Human-made spirit art, live performers, and cue-driven moments make the fight visible all day. Soul Torrent is the Saturday product we’re building toward; Sunday stays Tailgate and Big Game watch energy. Want to help unlock it? See Fund The Festival.

faq.q: What's a spot in a custom zone?
faq.a: One mapped 10×10 tent pad inside your zone. The baseline also includes the **plaza in front of the spot row** — open area for photos and mini programming. Bring popup shade (or add **frame tent** rental). A zone spot is not an assigned vendor-ring booth.

faq.q: Can I BYO popup tents and still get zone lighting?
faq.a: Yes — popup shade is fine. String lighting installs on **frame tents**, a **festival pole kit**, or **ground uplights** — festival staff rig and strike; we do not hang lights on popups.

faq.q: Why rent a zone instead of three vendor spots?
faq.a: Three vendor registrations get you three commerce spots in the vendor ring. A custom zone gives you adjacent spots **plus the plaza in front** — a named corner where your community can linger.

faq.q: Is this the same as Children’s Village or Maker Spot?
faq.a: No. Those are **preferred-provider RFPs** for kids / tween programming the festival product owns. Custom zones are **named corners** for community tribes and organizers who want identity on the map. Open RFPs live on the RFPs page.

faq.q: Are Tailgate camps the same as custom zones?
faq.a: No. Sunday **camps** are jersey-crew patches by the Big Game screen inside Kloss. Custom zones are themed villages / plazas elsewhere on the map — different product, different intake.

faq.q: Do festival organizers book singers for my zone?
faq.a: Not for LNY 2027. Microstage add-ons cover portable PA and plaza seating only. You bring your own performers and run-of-show — karaoke crew, church singers, community talent.

faq.q: Can we rent a zone if we're not Vietnamese-led?
faq.a: Yes — activation zones are for any tribe with a community and an identity to express. Cross-community villages (e.g. Chinese, Filipino, Russian) are welcome.
